title: String Quartet in C major, Op. 76 No. 3, “Emperor”
hook: Haydn’s hymn for the emperor, passed from one player to the next.

painting.title: Laxenburg from the Münkendorf Pavilion, looking south-west
painting.pairingNote: Painted for the imperial palace at Laxenburg, near Vienna, it shows a court hunting party crossing a wide, calm plain, the Habsburg world for which Haydn wrote his hymn to the emperor.

facts: Haydn wrote the quartet in 1797, aged 65, after his second stay in London. It is the third of six quartets dedicated to the Hungarian Count Joseph Erdődy, published in 1799 as his Op. 76.

The slow movement is a set of variations on *Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser* (“God save Franz the Emperor”), a hymn Haydn had just written for Emperor Francis II. It was first sung on the emperor’s birthday, 12 February 1797, at the Burgtheater in Vienna. According to a later account, Haydn had heard *God Save the King* in England and wanted his own country to have a song like it.
The tune outlived the empire. With new words written in 1841, it became the melody of the German national anthem, which is still sung today.
Haydn loved the hymn. In his last years he often played it at the piano, and his servant wrote that it was the last music Haydn ever played.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a bright Allegro with a rustic dance in the middle (I), the hymn and four variations (II), a sturdy minuet with a minor-key trio (III), a stormy finale that only finds C major at the end (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A bright, busy first movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]]. It grows from a short opening figure that passes between all four players, and in the middle it suddenly turns into a rough country dance.

mainIdeas.name: The opening figure
mainIdeas.description: five notes in the first violin, falling and rising, firm and clear. One scholar has read them as a hidden greeting to the emperor.

mainIdeas.name: The country dance
mainIdeas.description: a stamping tune over a held, droning bass, like a bagpipe.

stops.hear: The first violin plays a short, firm figure; the others answer and take it up
The opening figure again
The figure moves into new keys and is tossed between the instruments
The viola and cello hold a droning bass, like a bagpipe; the violins play a stamping country dance above it
stops.happening: A rustic dance over a [[pedal-note|pedal note]]

stops.hear: The opening figure returns in the home key
The development begins again, with its country dance

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: All four players together, in firm chords

notice: Follow the opening figure from player to player. In a quartet nobody is only an accompanist for long.
The country dance is a surprise in a serious piece. Listen for the drone that holds it down.

movements.heading: Poco adagio, cantabile
movements.summary: The hymn, then four variations on it. In this kind of [[variation|variation]] the tune itself hardly changes; instead it passes from player to player, and each time the others weave new music around it.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a slow, dignified tune in the first violin, with the other three in plain, full chords.

mainIdeas.name: The variations
mainIdeas.description: the tune moves to the second violin, then the cello, then the viola, and finally back to the first violin.

stops.hear: The first violin plays the slow hymn; the others support it in chords
stops.happening: The theme: *Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser*

stops.hear: Only two instruments: the second violin plays the hymn while the first violin twists quick, light lines around it
The hymn in the cello, deep and warm; the others weave above it
The hymn in the viola, in the middle of the texture; the harmonies grow darker
The first violin has the hymn again, now over richer, shifting harmonies

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The music slows and fades on a quiet chord

notice: In every variation, find the hymn first. It is always there, unchanged, in one of the four instruments.
In Variation 3 the tune is in the viola, the quartet’s middle voice. Try to hear it through the lines above and below.

movements.heading: Menuetto: Allegro
movements.summary: A sturdy, good-humoured [[minuet|minuet]] in C major, with a [[trio|trio]] that moves into A minor and a more shadowed mood.

stops.hear: A firm, cheerful dance for all four players
Quieter and darker, in a minor key
The cheerful dance returns

notice: Compare the trio’s minor-key colour with the minuet around it. The contrast prepares the dark opening of the finale.

movements.heading: Finale: Presto
movements.summary: A fast, fierce finale in [[sonata-form|sonata form]] that begins not in C major but in C minor, with three hammered chords. The bright home key is reached only near the end.

mainIdeas.name: The hammered chords
mainIdeas.description: three loud chords that open the movement and come back as a signal.

mainIdeas.name: The driving rhythm
mainIdeas.description: quick notes in groups of three that keep the music pressing forward.

stops.hear: Three loud, hammered chords, then fast, urgent music in the minor
stops.happening: The finale begins in C minor

stops.hear: The hammered chords again
Restless music moving through new keys
The opening chords and the urgent music return, still in the minor
The music turns to C major and brightens
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]: the major key arrives at last

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: All four players hammer out the final major chords

notice: Notice how long Haydn holds back the major key. When it arrives, it feels earned.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: This was the Takács Quartet’s first album for Decca, released in 1988, with the founding leader Gábor Takács-Nagy as first violin.

threads.title: The hymn
threads.body: The slow movement gives each of the four players a turn with the tune.

threads.title: Shared voices
threads.body: In the first movement too, the opening figure passes between all the instruments.

threads.title: From minor to major
threads.body: The trio’s minor key and the finale’s stormy C minor make the final arrival of C major sound like a victory.
